```{r packages, message=FALSE}
library("naboer")
library("tibble")
library("mgcv")

have_gratia <- requireNamespace("gratia", quietly = TRUE)
if (have_gratia) {
  library("gratia")
  library("ggplot2")
}

have_tsibble <- requireNamespace("tsibble", quietly = TRUE)
if (have_tsibble) {
  library("tsibble")
}
```

## Choose smoothness for a time series

We want a smooth that describes how soil moisture changed through 2019 at
Balruddery, near Dundee. Soil moisture on successive days is often similar.
A leave-one-out fit can use neighbouring days to predict a held-out day,
which can favour a smooth that follows short-term fluctuations. We will
compare that fit with one that also leaves out nearby days during smoothness
selection.

Read the 365 daily measurements from the COSMOS-UK monitoring network. The
`date` column defines the neighbourhoods. The number of days since 1 January
is the predictor in the model, and `vwc` is the volumetric water content as
a percentage. Contains data supplied by UK Centre for Ecology & Hydrology.
[COSMOS-UK data and licence](https://doi.org/10.5285/dde10e2b-ee1a-4b2b-a247-176db2f7bb31).

```{r soil-data}
soil <- read.csv(
  system.file("extdata", "balruddery-2019.csv", package = "naboer", mustWork = TRUE)
)
soil$date <- as.Date(soil$date)
soil$day <- as.numeric(soil$date - min(soil$date))
```

Make one fold per day. In each fold, leave out the target day and up to 20
days on either side, and score the prediction for the target day alone.
This window follows the example in David L. Miller's article. The appropriate
window for another series depends on how long residual dependence persists.
[Miller's time-series example](https://calgary.converged.yt/articles/ncv_timeseries.html#what-about-restricting-the-prediction-neighbourhood).

```{r soil-folds}
soil_folds <- neighbourhoods(soil,
  index = date, temporal = temporal_window(time_span(20, "days"))
)
```

Check a fold in the middle of the year. To score 2 July, the fit leaves out
12 June to 22 July inclusive.

```{r inspect-soil-fold}
soil_data <- fold_data(soil_folds)
july_fold <- match(as.Date("2019-07-02"), soil_data$date)
range(soil_data$date[omission_indices(soil_folds, july_fold)[[1]]])
```

Fit the same smooth twice with mgcv. With `nei` omitted, `method = "NCV"`
uses leave-one-out cross-validation. For the second fit, export the temporal
folds with `as_nei()` and supply that design as `nei`. Both fits use the same
data and basis, so the change is in how the smoothing parameter is selected.

```{r soil-fits}
soil_loo <- gam(vwc ~ s(day, k = 20),
  data = soil_data, method = "NCV", na.action = na.fail
)

soil_nei <- as_nei(soil_folds, data = soil_data)
soil_ncv <- gam(vwc ~ s(day, k = 20),
  data = soil_data, method = "NCV", nei = soil_nei, na.action = na.fail
)
```

Compare the effective degrees of freedom (EDF) of the smooth. Higher EDF
allows the curve to follow more fluctuations in the data.

```{r soil-edf}
c(
  `Leave-one-out` = summary(soil_loo)$s.table[1, "edf"],
  `Temporal neighbourhoods` = summary(soil_ncv)$s.table[1, "edf"]
)
```

Use gratia's `add_fitted()` to add each model's fitted moisture values to
the observed dates. Both final models use all 365 observations.

```{r soil-curve-data, eval=have_gratia}
soil_curves <- rbind(
  transform(add_fitted(soil_data, soil_loo, value = "fitted_vwc"),
    scheme = "Leave-one-out"
  ),
  transform(add_fitted(soil_data, soil_ncv, value = "fitted_vwc"),
    scheme = "Temporal neighbourhoods"
  )
)
```

Overlay the two fitted curves on the observations in grey. The neighbourhood
fit follows the broader changes in moisture over the year.

```{r soil-curves, eval=have_gratia, fig.width=7, fig.height=4, dev.args=list(bg="white"), fig.alt="Daily soil moisture at Balruddery in grey and two fitted curves. The temporal neighbourhood fit is smoother than the leave-one-out fit."}
ggplot(soil_data, aes(x = date)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = vwc), colour = "grey60", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(
    data = soil_curves,
    aes(y = fitted_vwc, colour = scheme, linetype = scheme),
    linewidth = 0.9
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    "Leave-one-out" = "#D55E00", "Temporal neighbourhoods" = "#0072B2"
  )) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(
    "Leave-one-out" = "dashed", "Temporal neighbourhoods" = "solid"
  )) +
  labs(
    x = "Date in 2019", y = "Volumetric water content (%)",
    colour = NULL, linetype = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The two-sided window selects a smooth for the observed period. Forecasting
uses an information cut-off, described later in this article.

## Multiple time series

When you have several time series, decide whether observations at the same
time in different series should be held out together. For example, two
monitoring sites might respond to the same weather. You might want to hold
out both sites to assess predictions for a new period.

### Set up the time series

Create daily records for two sites. In these examples, `site` is the key
that identifies each series and `date` is the time index. Supplying a key
keeps track of the series. Use `.by` separately when the data contain
independent domains and the design should keep neighbourhoods within them.

```{r example-data}
x <- tibble(
  site = rep(c("a", "b"), each = 12),
  date = rep(as.Date("2024-01-01") + 0:11, 2)
)
```

### Leave out observations near each target

Use `neighbourhoods()` to assess one row per fold. A two-day window leaves out
the target and any observations up to two days before or after it. Here
`within = "key"` restricts that window to the target's site. Use
`within = "domain"` to include nearby dates from both sites when they
belong to the same domain.

```{r temporal-neighbourhoods}
f <- neighbourhoods(x,
  key = site, index = date, within = "key",
  temporal = temporal_window(time_span(2, "days"))
)
```

Inspect the rows omitted in fold 3. The target is 3 January at site a, so
the model leaves out 1 to 5 January at that site and scores only 3 January.

```{r inspect-neighbourhood}
fold_data(f)[omission_indices(f, 3)[[1]], ]
```

### Choose how to measure a span

- **Elapsed time** is measured in seconds. An elapsed day is 86,400 seconds.
  Numeric time indices are also interpreted in seconds.
- **Calendar time** follows the local calendar. Across a daylight-saving
  change, a calendar day can be 23 or 25 hours. When shifting by months or
  years, a date that would fall past the end of a month moves to its last day.
  Calendar shifts preserve the time of day, including fractional seconds,
  subject to the chosen daylight-saving rules. naboer uses `clock` for this
  calendar arithmetic.
- **Observation counts** measure a span in recorded rows. Blocks start at
  the first row of each series, and neighbourhoods count away from the target.
  Use `time_span(2, "observations")` for a span of two rows and
  set `within = "key"`. Resolve tied times in each series before using counts.
  Time-based windows can include observations with the same timestamp.

Temporal windows include observations on both boundaries. Elapsed windows
allow for rounding when calculating time differences at a boundary. When
calendar arithmetic would reach a repeated or skipped local clock time,
the calculation fails by default. Use the `ambiguous` or `nonexistent`
argument of `time_span()` to choose how to resolve those times. A zero-length
shift preserves the original timestamp, including which occurrence of a
repeated time it represents. For date-times, calendar arithmetic uses the
time zone of the index even if supplied origins are displayed in a different
zone.

## Hold out whole periods

To assess a new period at both sites, use `temporal_folds()` with
`within = "domain"`. Start the four-day blocks on 1 January.

```{r make-blocks}
blocks <- temporal_folds(x, time_span(4, "days"),
  key = site, index = date,
  within = "domain", origin = as.Date("2024-01-01")
)
```

The fold summary shows three blocks of eight assessment rows each, four
from each site.

```{r inspect-blocks}
as_tibble(blocks)
```

A time-based block includes its start and excludes its end, so 5 January
belongs to the second block. If you omit `origin`, each domain or series
starts at its earliest observation. Count-based blocks start at the first
observation of each series and take no `origin` argument.

## Assess forecasts using information available at the time

A forecasting fold has a cut-off called the *origin*. Here the model can use
records through the origin. The gap is the period after the origin when no
predictions are scored. The horizon is the period immediately after the gap
when predictions are scored. Later records, including those beyond the
horizon, are left out of training.

Generate the first origin three elapsed days after the first observation.
Move the origin forward by two days at a time, the default step when the
horizon is two days. With multiple series in one domain, time-based forecasts
use a shared origin so neither site's future records enter the fit.

```{r make-forecast-folds}
forecast <- forecast_folds(x,
  initial = time_span(3, "days"),
  horizon = time_span(2, "days"), gap = time_span(1, "days"),
  key = site, index = date
)
```

Inspect the first fold. Both sites contribute training records from 1 to
4 January. The records on 5 January form the gap, and the predictions for
6 and 7 January are scored.

```{r inspect-first-forecast}
forecast_data <- fold_data(forecast)
forecast_data[analysis_indices(forecast, 1)[[1]], ]
forecast_data[assessment_indices(forecast, 1)[[1]], ]
```

Training starts with the first observation by default. For a fixed training
history, set `window = "sliding"` and supply a `lookback` span. Training then
uses times strictly after `origin - lookback` and through the origin.

Generated origins require the horizon to end on or before the last observed
time in the domain. Series can end earlier or have gaps, and generated
horizons with no observations to assess are skipped. To choose cut-off dates
yourself, supply `origins` in place of `initial`. Each explicit origin must
leave at least one training and one assessment row in every domain.

When both `initial` and `step` are calendar spans measured in months or years,
origins are calculated from the first observation's date to keep month-end
and leap-day adjustments from carrying over to later origins. The same
anchoring applies when both spans use calendar days or weeks. The daylight-saving
rules in `initial` apply to the first origin, and those in `step` apply
to later origins.

### Forecast across separate domains

Observation-count forecasts require a single series per domain. For related
series recorded at different times, use elapsed or calendar spans so there is a
common time cut-off. Forecasting with `within = "key"` also requires a single
series per domain.

Setting `.by = site` gives each site its own forecast schedule and leaves records
from other sites available for fitting, including their later records. If the
same cut-off should apply to both sites, keep them in one domain
as above.

### Refit models at forecast origins

When refitting at each origin, construct predictors and estimate missing
values using only information available at that time. Forecast folds often
leave out many observations. If you use neighbourhood cross-validation
(NCV) instead of explicit refitting, compare the approximation with exact
refits for your model and forecast folds. See the
[comparison with exact refits](naboer.html#check-the-approximation-for-large-omissions).

## Use a tsibble

With an ordinary tibble, supply `key` and `index` explicitly. With a tsibble,
naboer reads them from the object. If you have `tsibble` installed, convert
the example data and use `within = "key"` to make four-day blocks separately
for each site.

```{r tsibble, eval=have_tsibble}
series <- as_tsibble(x, key = site, index = date)
temporal_folds(series, time_span(4, "days"), within = "key")
```

For tsibble indices that represent weeks, months or quarters, temporal
calculations use the first date of each period. `fold_data()` keeps the
original index class.
